clue.text: Gray in darkness here ?

parts.note: Thomas Gray's Elegy is set in a country churchyard where the ploughman 'leaves the world to darkness and to me'; the clue asks for that village

explanation.surface: A question about where a grey shade might be found in the dark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gray' looks like a colour but is the poet Thomas Gray, whose Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard was set in this Buckinghamshire village and whose first stanza ends in darkness.
explanation.definitionFit: The Buckinghamshire churchyard of this village is the traditional setting of the poet's famous elegy.

clue.text: Fish out of river is found in ditch

indicators.note: the fish is placed outside the river abbreviation, so it wraps around it

parts.note: the tench is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A fish taken from a river ends up lying in a ditch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' reads as removal, but here it means the fish sits on the outside: TENCH wraps R to give T-R-ENCH.
explanation.definitionFit: A trench is a long narrow dug channel, the same thing as a ditch.

clue.text: In Nagasaki low-attack aircraft in current production

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of words that follows, spanning the word join

explanation.surface: A wartime picture of ground-attack planes over a Japanese city.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 'NagasaKI LOW-ATTack'; the aircraft talk is surface dressing, and 'current production' means the output of electric current.
explanation.definitionFit: A thousand watts is a unit of electrical power, the rate at which electric current does work.

clue.text: Flower that's picked, but not, in short, by the square-toed

definitions.meaning: a blue-flowered trailing plant of the genus Vinca

definitions.text: that's picked, but not, in short, by the square-toed
definitions.meaning: the sea snail also called a winkle is picked out with a pin, and pointed shoes are 'winkle-pickers', which no square-toed shoe is

explanation.surface: A flower gathered by everyone except people wearing blunt-toed shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in short' cuts the name of the sea snail down to winkle, and winkle-pickers are sharply pointed shoes, so the square-toed are not they.
explanation.definitionFit: The name covers both a blue garden plant of the Vinca family and an edible sea snail, the winkle.

clue.text: Fowler's hunting, shooting and fishing, for example

definitions.text: Fowler's hunting, shooting and fishing, for example

parts.words: Fowler's hunting, shooting and fishing, for example
parts.note: H. W. Fowler wrote Modern English Usage; to the grammarian, words like 'hunting' used as nouns are a part of speech, not field sports

explanation.surface: A bird-catcher's country pursuits listed: hunting, shooting and fishing.
explanation.walkthrough: A fowler is a bird-hunter, but this Fowler is H. W. Fowler, author of Modern English Usage, who would class these -ing words grammatically.
explanation.definitionFit: Verbal nouns ending in -ing, used as the names of activities, are what grammarians call by this term.

clue.text: Discern the point on which one faces danger

definitions.meaning: to discern is to notice or catch sight of

definitions.text: the point on which one faces danger
definitions.meaning: being 'on the' place of trouble is to be in a difficult position

explanation.surface: Learning to recognise the moment when danger arrives.
explanation.definitionFit: To notice something is to pick it out; and 'in a tight place' is to be on this, a difficult position.

clue.text: In a cold wind one finds no justice

indicators.note: the numeral for one goes in the middle of the wind's name

parts.note: the mistral is a cold north wind of southern France
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone out in a bitter wind laments that there is no justice.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial voided by an error yields no proper verdict, so justice is not done.

clue.text: Tough at the top

parts.note: read as 'hard in the head': a person tough in the head is shrewd and unsentimental

explanation.surface: The old saying that life is hard for those in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase recalls 'it's tough at the top', but read literally it is hard at the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Being practical and unsentimental is being tough-minded, literally hard in the head.

clue.text: Irishman in a film

parts.note: Pat is the stock name for an Irishman
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Irish actor appearing in a movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'film' suggests a movie but means a thin surface layer.
explanation.definitionFit: A patina is a thin coating that forms on old metal or wood.

clue.text: A rare store-keeper, Simon

parts.note: the Victorian song 'Old Simon the ...' tells of a man who keeps a rare store of good malmsey and Malvoisie in his wine vaults

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper named Simon is an unusual man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rare' seems to describe the man, but in the old song it is his store of wine that is rare.
explanation.definitionFit: The officer in charge of a monastery's wine and provisions keeps the stores, like old Simon of the song.

clue.text: Had honey remained so, Jonathan had not been imperilled

definitions.text: Had honey remained so, Jonathan had not been imperilled

parts.words: Had honey remained so, Jonathan had not been imperilled
parts.note: in 1 Samuel 14 Jonathan dipped his rod in honey and ate it, breaking his father Saul's oath, and was condemned to die

explanation.surface: A biblical what-if about Jonathan and some honey.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1 Samuel 14 Saul swore that no soldier would eat before evening; Jonathan ate honey unawares and Saul would have had him killed.
explanation.definitionFit: Honey nobody had eaten from would be untouched, never sampled, and Jonathan would have been safe.

clue.text: Among the gunners he gets the bird

indicators.note: the pronoun is placed in the middle of the soldiers' abbreviation

parts.note: RA, the Royal Artillery, are the army's gunners
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man in an artillery unit is sent off with a jeer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets the bird' sounds like being booed, but the bird is the definition: the South American ostrich-like flightless bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhea is a large flightless South American bird related to the ostrich.

clue.text: Something dicky with the car, causing a noise ?

definitions.text: Something dicky with the car, causing a noise ?

parts.words: Something dicky with the car, causing a noise
parts.note: a 'dicky' is the folding back seat of an old two-seater; the clue suggests a fault that makes a rumble

explanation.surface: A motorist hears a worrying noise from a faulty car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dicky' is British slang for faulty, but it is also the old name for a folding seat at the back of a car, and a rumble is a noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A folding open-air seat at the back of an early car, also called a dicky.

clue.text: Used by Benares metal-workers one after the other ?

definitions.meaning: a rasping tool from India, as used by the brass-workers of Benares (Varanasi)
walking in single line, each behind the one in front

explanation.surface: A craft workshop where Indian metalsmiths work in turn.
explanation.walkthrough: Benares (now Varanasi) was famous for brassware, so its workers would use an Indian rasp, read literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Walking in single column is the old phrase from Native American trails; and literally a rasping tool from India.

clue.text: Two music-hall Harrys combine to make inferior variety

indicators.note: the two surnames are mixed together into one new word

parts.note: Harry Lauder was a Scottish music-hall singer
Harry Tate was an English music-hall comedian

explanation.surface: Two variety comedians team up to put on a poorer show.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Lauder and Harry Tate were stars of British music hall; 'combine' rearranges LAUDER and TATE together. 'variety' plays on music hall's other name.
explanation.definitionFit: To adulterate is to debase something by adding a cheaper substance, lowering its quality.

clue.text: Ski team's boob ?

indicators.note: a blunder throws the letters of the first two words out of order

parts.note: the possessive adds no letter

explanation.surface: A skiing squad makes a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boob' is both the definition and the sign that SKI TEAM is jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: A boob is British slang for an error or blunder.

clue.text: She has to desert the furniture man

parts.note: taken as written
to rat on someone is to desert or betray them

explanation.surface: A woman has to leave the furniture maker.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Sheraton was an 18th-century English furniture designer.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Sheraton was the English cabinet-maker whose name labels a style of furniture.

clue.text: Retired attired

parts.note: the old courting custom in which a couple went to bed together fully clothed

explanation.surface: Going to bed with one's clothes on.
explanation.walkthrough: Bundling was an old courting custom in which a courting couple shared a bed fully dressed.
explanation.definitionFit: A couple who bundled went to bed together while still dressed, the old courting custom.

clue.text: Columbine End ? What a joint !

parts.note: columbine means dove-like, from Latin columba, a dove
the tail is the end of something

explanation.surface: Columbine, the pantomime character, takes a bow and someone admires a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Columbine is a pantomime character, but the word also means 'of a dove'; 'joint' is not a pub but a woodworking joint.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodworking interlock of fan-shaped tenons that fit into matching mortises.

clue.text: But this sweet cake is no sponge

definitions.text: But this sweet cake is no sponge

parts.words: But this sweet cake is no sponge
parts.note: the clue links a bath, where one uses a sponge, with a sweet bun that is not a sponge cake

explanation.surface: A remark that this particular sweet treat is not a sponge cake.
explanation.walkthrough: Sponges belong in the bath, so one would expect this item to be a sponge; but the bun named after the city of Bath is a yeasted bun, not a sponge cake.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet sugar-topped currant bun first made in the English spa city of Bath.

clue.text: One who holds his place in the army

definitions.text: One who holds his place in the army

parts.words: One who holds his place in the army
parts.note: the French lieu, place, and tenant, holding: an officer who holds a place in place of a superior

explanation.surface: A soldier who keeps his position in the ranks.
explanation.walkthrough: The rank's name is French for 'place-holding': lieu, place, plus tenant, holding.
explanation.definitionFit: The rank's name comes from French for place-holder, a deputy acting in a superior's stead.

clue.text: Sell a few at last

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral five, taken as a small number
the end is the last part

explanation.surface: A trader finally manages to sell a few items.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a few' stands for a small number, here five, V in Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: To vend is to offer goods for sale.

clue.text: Hearts are broken in clue construction

indicators.note: the letters of the next two words are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A crossword setter's heart breaks when building a clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges IN CLUE; 'construction' completes the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuclei are central cores, as hearts are the centres of things.

clue.text: To hit and run is hardly workmanlike

parts.note: to slap is to hit with the open hand
to dash is to run fast

explanation.surface: A hit-and-run driver is criticised for shoddy behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hit and run' suggests a traffic crime, but it is two verbs placed side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Careless, hurried work is anything but the careful work of a good craftsman.

clue.text: Help Lincoln at the finish

parts.note: Abe is short for Abraham Lincoln

indicators.note: the finish of the word 'at' is its last letter

explanation.surface: Coming to Abraham Lincoln's aid at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To abet is to assist or encourage, usually in wrongdoing.

clue.text: Farmland may …, unlike the last straw

definitions.meaning: fill the gap with two words: farmland may be fit for ploughing
the last straw is proverbially more than one can endure

explanation.surface: Farmland can be ploughed, though the final straw is more than anyone can take.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap takes BE ARABLE, two words run together; the last straw breaks the camel's back, so it is the opposite of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Land that can be ploughed 'be arable'; and something tolerable is what the last straw is not.

clue.text: A river horse is way out of this world!

parts.note: the Po is the longest river in Italy
gee, or gee-gee, is a child's word for a horse

explanation.surface: A hippopotamus is called extraordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'river horse' suggests a hippo but splits into two pieces; 'way out of this world' is the point of an orbit farthest from Earth.
explanation.definitionFit: The apogee is the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.

clue.text: Undercut part of New York

definitions.meaning: the undercut is the tender cut of beef from under the ribs
a Manhattan district once notorious for vice

explanation.surface: Someone underprices a section of New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undercut' looks like a verb but is the butcher's name for the fillet; the second sense is a Manhattan district.
explanation.definitionFit: The undercut is the tender fillet of beef, and the Manhattan red-light district bore the same name.
